sourceBindings.text: Two cups are not a mass reading
The example says submit 'about 2 cups or 500 grams' of the composite.
Ask what amount and unit the receiving lab actually requests.
If it requires 500 g, weigh that amount; if it requests two cups, measure volume and label it as such.
Record the sample ID and required sampling depth/count rather than equating volume with mass.
One unambiguous measured submission amount and an intact identity chain.

sourceBindings.text: A ratio must name its basis

The teaching example uses 20 g dry soil plus 20 mL distilled water: mass:volume. A separate laboratory method uses 1:1 volume:volume, taking soil with the scoop named ‘10 gram NCR-13 volumetric scoop’ and adding 10 mL deionized water. That is a volumetric scoop's name, not an instruction to weigh exactly 10 g of this soil.
The worked example is mass:volume; the lab example is volume:volume.
Choose the actual training SOP and meter, then log its aliquot, wait and calibration; do not borrow an attractive number from the other procedure.
A digital-electrode measurement and a colour-reagent comparison use different equipment and procedures; one does not demonstrate the other.
A reproducible, device-matched measurement rather than a mixed-method number.

sourceBindings.text: The same short ribbon may mean different classes
Two samples both produce a 2 cm ribbon, but one feels gritty and the other feels very smooth when wet rubbed.
Confirm proper moisture and ball/ribbon conditions first.
Follow the USDA weak-ribbon branch, then distinguish gritty from smooth wet-rub feel.

If the weak-ribbon sample feels very gritty, the guide supports sandy loam; if it feels very smooth, it supports silt loam. If neither feel predominates, use the loam branch. These remain conditional field estimates.
Classify with both ribbon length and feel; note field-estimate uncertainty.
